Normal: Ordinary, legitimate traffic from everyday operation of devices and applications, such as sensor readings, protocol messages between IoT components, web requests and DNS lookups. It generally shows regular communication patterns, complete connection handshakes and moderate traffic rates. It does not contain floods, scans or malicious payloads.
Backdoor: Malware or a planted mechanism that gives an attacker hidden remote access to a device, avoiding normal authentication. On the network it often appears as unexpected outbound connections to a controlling server or a device listening on unusual ports. Traffic tends to be low in volume but persistent, with periodic beaconing and bursts when commands or data are exchanged.
Password: An attack that tries to obtain valid credentials by guessing, for example by brute force or dictionary methods against a login service. On the network it appears as many repeated authentication attempts from one source in a short time, most of them failing. Success gives the attacker legitimate-looking access to the device or application.
DDoS_HTTP: A distributed attack in which many sources send a very large number of HTTP requests to a web server. Each request can look like normal web traffic, but the combined volume uses up the server's connections and processing capacity. On the network it appears as a sudden surge of HTTP requests to one target from many addresses.
DDoS_ICMP: A distributed attack in which many sources send a flood of ICMP packets, typically echo requests (pings), to a target. The target has to process and often answer each one, which consumes bandwidth and CPU. On the network it appears as an abnormally high rate of ICMP traffic reaching one destination from many sources.
DDoS_UDP: A distributed attack in which many sources send a very large number of UDP packets to a target, often across many ports. Because UDP is connectionless, the target has to examine each packet and may reply with ICMP unreachable messages, using up resources. On the network it appears as a heavy surge of UDP traffic aimed at a single host.
DDoS_TCP: A distributed attack in which many sources send an overwhelming number of TCP packets, often connection requests such as SYN packets, to a target. The target spends bandwidth, CPU and connection-table space handling them. On the network it appears as a sustained, abnormally high rate of TCP traffic toward one destination from many addresses.
MITM: A man-in-the-middle attack in which the attacker secretly positions themselves between two communicating devices so they can read or alter the traffic. A common method is forging ARP messages so that traffic is redirected through the attacker's machine. On the network it can appear as conflicting or unsolicited ARP replies and an IP address that suddenly maps to a different MAC address.
OS_Fingerprinting: A reconnaissance technique that sends specially crafted packets to a device and studies how it responds in order to guess its operating system. Differences in how systems handle certain packets and options act as a fingerprint. On the network it appears as a series of unusual or varied probes to one host, often combined with port probing.
Port_Scanning: A reconnaissance technique that tries to connect to many ports on a target to find which are open and which services are running. It is usually an early step before an attack on a discovered service. On the network it appears as many short connection attempts from one source to numerous different ports on the same host, often with many refused or unanswered.
Vulnerability_scanner: An automated process that probes devices and services for known weaknesses such as outdated software or misconfigurations. It is often a preparation step before an actual exploit. On the network it appears as many varied requests to different ports and services from one source in a short time, often following patterns typical of scanning tools.
SQL_injection: An attack in which malicious SQL code is placed into input fields or request parameters of a web application so the back-end database runs it. It can expose, change or delete stored data, or bypass login checks. On the network it appears as web requests whose parameters contain SQL keywords, quotes and special characters.
XSS: Cross-site scripting, an attack in which malicious script code is inserted into a web page or request so that it runs in another user's browser. It can be used to steal session data, redirect users or change what the page shows. On the network it appears as web requests or responses containing script tags or encoded script content in parameters.
Uploading: An attack in which the attacker uploads a malicious file, such as a script or web shell, to a vulnerable web application or device. If the server accepts and runs the file, the attacker can gain control over it. On the network it appears as HTTP upload requests carrying unexpected file types or content, often followed by requests to run the uploaded file.
Ransomware: Malware that locks or encrypts a victim's files or systems and demands payment for restoring access. Before and during an infection it may contact an external controlling server and may try to spread to other devices on the network. On the network this can appear as unusual outbound connections, scanning or spreading activity, and heavy file-access traffic.
